passage: Hrithik, I saw you punch your pillow after that phone call. Let your Chandrika Bua tell you about being fifteen. I had a temper like a pressure cooker. One day my best friend Shobha laughed at my poem in front of the whole class. I came home and wrote her a letter so cruel my hand shook. I was running to the post box when my father said, "Post it tomorrow if you still want to." That evening I went up to the terrace and skipped rope till my legs burned, then poured everything into my diary. By morning the letter looked like someone else had written it. I tore it up and told Shobha, calmly, that she had hurt me. She said sorry. We are still friends, two old women now. Feelings are storms, beta. They pass.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling as she wrote the letter?
qa.a: She felt furious and humiliated, so angry that her hand shook.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chandrika's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Waiting overnight at her father's suggestion and letting the anger out through skipping and her diary; by morning she could talk to Shobha calmly instead of sending something she would regret.

qa.q: How might Shobha have been affected if the cruel letter had been posted?
qa.a: She would have been deeply hurt, and a friendship that lasted into old age might have ended.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that big feelings pass, using exercise and writing as outlets, and waiting before sending something in anger.

passage: The night before the maths exam, rain hammered the Kochi flat and the power kept flickering. Then Mehak saw it: Thomas had posted her old mispronunciation video in the class group, with three laughing faces. Her face burned. She typed fast: "You're pathetic and everyone knows it." Her thumb hovered over send. Instead she set a timer for an hour and threw the phone onto her bed. The rain was too heavy for her usual run, so she put on loud music and danced round her room till she was breathless, then wrote everything in her notebook, ugly words included. When the timer rang, she deleted the draft and messaged Thomas privately: "That video really embarrassed me. Please take it down." Soon it was gone, with a "sorry, didn't think". She went back to her maths.

qa.q: How long did Mehak set the timer for?
What was Mehak feeling when she saw the video?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious; her face burned and she typed a cruel reply.

qa.q: Which of Mehak's choices prevented regret, and why?
qa.a: Waiting an hour, dancing and writing out the anger before replying, so she sent a calm, clear request instead of an insult.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt receiving the calm message instead of the insult?
qa.a: Thomas could see the hurt clearly without getting defensive, which made it easy to apologise and take the video down.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with a storm of feelings finding outlets in music, movement and writing, and waiting an hour before sending a message.
